rationale: A wins because it keeps its hands clean: "Whatnot hit $3B in sales — so what do its sellers actually take home?" is a real reporter question and it names the missing proof before anyone gets cute. B has sharper tabloid energy, but "A private company with $3B in sales and a $5B valuation is worth less than one times revenue it doesn't keep" is math-mangled and built on a line Whatnot did not provide. The difference is discipline: A interrogates the update; B starts recruiting extra facts to make the room louder.
gaps_in_A: "the data so far says they don't" overstates the record. The update says Asia is larger and Whatnot is betting the US catches up; it does not provide data proving US shoppers reject the behavior.
"the first hard data point that the format scales past collectors" is too confident without the collectibles-versus-fashion/electronics split the set itself admits is missing.

"Whatnot's $5B valuation makes it a livestream-commerce unicorn" is rightly refused, but A may have left a narrower GMV-vs-revenue valuation mechanics angle on the table if the valuation date and take-rate can be substantiated.
gaps_in_B: "The $3B figure is gross merchandise volume" is not supplied. The update says annual livestream-commerce sales; the definition is exactly what needs proving.

"eBay, Poshmark-style resale, and consumer-electronics resale volume moves" invents competitive and resale context. Fashion and electronics are in the update; those incumbents and market-share stakes are not.
"worth less than one times revenue it doesn't keep" is a bad line. $5B against $3B is not less than 1x, and the $3B is not established as revenue in the first place.
"shutdown-and-retreat cycle of Western live-shopping efforts" may be true beat context, but it is not in the update and needs sourcing. As written, it behaves like a fake peg.
